title: Global Reporting Regulation, Stock Liquidity, and Policy Diffusion
abstract: We study stock liquidity around 17 families of reporting regulation and their international diffusion. We distinguish national implementation from issuer eligibility and actual public reporting. The market panel contains 1,055,142 security-years in 90 jurisdictions. Source-supported comparisons cover seven first-year families and five balanced-window families. Their first-year log-spread contrasts are -0.077 with equal family weights and +0.187 with market-capitalisation family weights. Audit reporting receives 85.6% of the latter weight, equivalent to only 1.36 equally weighted families in concentration terms. An exact decomposition locates the difference in policy composition. First statutory reporting also follows voluntary disclosure in documented cases, limiting the information increment. Complementary liquidity outcomes and pre-policy differences constrain a general causal benefit. No diffusion coefficient survives broad multiplicity adjustment. The evidence identifies the importance of the policy mix, covered population and information timing when comparing reporting mandates.
sections: 1. Introduction

Reporting regulation can reduce adverse selection by supplying credible information. Its market effect should depend on the incremental information, the firms required to disclose and the audience receiving it. We ask how stock liquidity changes around reporting mandates and whether foreign policy choices help explain their diffusion. Combining mandates requires a further choice: whether the object is the average regulation family or the regulation exposure of large issuers.

Following the empirical logic of Krueger et al. (2023), we establish obligations and reporting dates before connecting them to issuer outcomes. The setting extends beyond comprehensive sustainability reporting to 17 economic regulation families. We then apply the competition, learning, emulation and coercion framework of Koning, Mertens and Roosenboom (2018). A national implementation date establishes geographic exposure; a covered-issuer study additionally needs evidence of the relevant issuer obligation or report.

The principal finding is that policy composition materially changes the aggregate spread contrast. Across seven source-supported families, equal-family and market-capitalisation weights yield -0.077 and +0.187, respectively. Audit reporting accounts for 85.6% of market-cap weight. We decompose the difference exactly and disclose every single-family exclusion, rather than select a favourable omission. First-year and longer-window support differ. The estimates therefore describe specified policy mixes, not a common causal reporting benefit.
2. Institutional setting and research design

A public report can change investor information; confidential CbCR submitted to tax authorities does not constitute the same public-information event. Comprehensive mandatory E/S/G requires a response on all three topics, with the final topic determining the joint date. CSR spending, climate-only rules and voluntary guidance are classified separately. The inherited topic review retains 37 qualifying phases from 41 country reviews; earliest separate topic histories remain incomplete. Bank public CbCR attaches to institutions and consolidation perimeters, not automatically every listed holding company.

Eligibility and information timing are rule specific (Table 1). The source-supported studies cover auditor reports, XBRL, conflict minerals, bank CbCR, IFRS, German statutory nonfinancial reports and extractive payments. BP, Total SA and Tullow report FY 2015 statutory payments in 2016. BP publishes on 24 June. Total states that its French registration document was filed on 16 March; the signature is dated 15 March. A contemporaneous SEC rule corroborates Tullow’s 15 March annual report. Tullow explicitly reports voluntarily since 2013. Rio Tinto’s June voluntary Taxes paid release does not establish the separate statutory filing date, which remains unresolved.

The 2000-2025 panel contains 99,100 vendor quote/company identifiers. Outcomes are log median relative quoted spread, log median Amihud price impact and the fraction of valid observed returns equal to zero. Each requires 120 valid observations; logged proxies use annual 1/99 winsorisation. These calendar-year measures differ from the reference study. Exact historical home-share identifiers and source reports corroborate the selected issuer matches; current company names alone do not establish historical legal entities.

For each family, cohort and endpoint, we subtract the weighted comparison change from the implementer change relative to g -1. Geographic comparisons require known later implementation, at least 30 issuers per country and three comparison markets. Source-supported comparisons require at least three treated and 20 comparison issuers. First-year contrasts use g -1 and g. Balanced support is fixed from g -3 through g +2 and averages years 0-2. Unknown histories are not coded never-treated. Few legal waves, selection and cross-market differences limit policy inference.

GDP in g -1 is allocated over the fixed source-study issuer universe within each country; cohorts are weighted by treated mass. Across economic families, equal weights assign 1/F and market-cap weights use pre-event treated issuer capitalisation. Both use the same supported family set for all outcomes, and banking enters once. Equal-issuer and issuer-cap within-family alternatives are disclosed. Market-cap exposure counts repeated issuer-policy observations and is not a unique-issuer portfolio.

Source candidates are selected by pre-event size before new coefficients are inspected. IFRS comparisons require US domestic-bank and auditor US GAAP evidence. German nonfinancial-report comparisons require US parent incorporation. Extractive comparisons use resource-sector parents with contemporaneous US incorporation/listing evidence, withholding direct foreign-regime flags. US payment rules were not operative in the 2016-18 window, but foreign subsidiaries and voluntary reporting remain possible. We review 164 additional full SEC filings; source and outcome failures remain visible. Issuer sampling intervals preserve shared-issuer covariance and do not supply causal policy confidence intervals.
3. Liquidity, information timing and policy composition

Table 2 Panel A reports geographic exposure. Fifteen first-year families yield equal-family spread -0.049 and price impact -0.072, compared with +0.015 and +0.009 under market-cap weights. Confidential tax CbCR receives 33.1% of that exposure weight. Nine families support the balanced window. Significant pre-policy spread differences and unresolved eligibility prevent interpreting these broad contrasts as effects on all legally covered issuers.

Panel B uses seven source-supported first-year families. Equal-family spread is -0.077; market-cap spread is +0.187. Price impact is +0.025 and +0.190, respectively. Figure 1 reports every family and its market-cap weight. The cap-weighted sample is concentrated: its effective family count, 1/sum(w squared), is 1.36. The cap-minus-equal spread difference is +0.264 log points. The downloadable decomposition attributes this difference to each family’s weight change times its fixed estimate, and reports every leave-one-family-out contrast. Reweighting changes the target population; it does not improve identification.

Table 3 identifies the individual studies. CAM has 1,481 treated and 2,767 comparison issuer-cohort observations, while early XBRL has six treated and 62 comparisons. The IFRS study contains four Canadian banks and 42 US comparisons; German statutory nonfinancial reporting contains three issuers and 35 comparisons. Their first-year spread contrasts are -0.235 and -0.217, but IFRS price impact increases. The source and comparison populations differ across these settings.

Extractive reporting extends support beyond six families. BP, Total and Tullow have three treated and 35 first-year comparisons, with spread +0.004, price impact +0.162 and zero-return fraction +0.00334. Balanced support retains 24 comparisons. Prior voluntary reporting at Tullow means the statutory cycle need not create wholly new information. Commodity prices, Brexit, the BP settlement and cross-country exposure also change in this window. We retain this study under both aggregate weights because source support, rather than the coefficient sign, determines inclusion.

Five families support balanced years 0-2: banks, conflict minerals, IFRS, German nonfinancial and extractive reports. Equal-family and market-cap spreads are -0.042 and -0.058, while price impact is +0.149 and +0.211. Figure 2 shows the fixed-sample profiles and material pre-policy differences. The shorter-window seven-family aggregate cannot be joined to this five-family series as a single dynamic effect. The evidence supports studying information increments and policy composition, while leaving a universal causal liquidity improvement unestablished.
4. International diffusion and conclusion

Following Koning et al., competition uses prior adoption among export-pattern peers; learning uses prior outcomes among geographic neighbours; emulation uses language, legal-origin and IGO peers; external dependence uses IMF credit and aid. Signals precede the focal decision. Family-year strata and country-clustered covariance accompany timing and status alternatives, with lagged income, growth and trade controls where specified. The ledger records documented phases rather than certified first-ever adoption.

Across 1,330 attempted designs, 433 stable focal coefficients remain and none survives the broad Holm correction. We refit the full matrix; additional issuer report dates do not create new national adoption decisions. Later liquidity estimates are not inserted into earlier learning signals. Reporting mandates differ in their information increments and covered economic mass. A comparison of those differences provides a coherent research question, while source coverage, pretrends and common legal waves constrain causal and diffusion claims.
